RSA encryption. RSA stands for Rivest-Shamir-Adleman, a public-key cryptographic algorithm that enables secure communication over insecure channels. It relies on the mathematical difficulty of factoring large composite numbers. A number that is trivial to verify as a product of two large primes is computationally hard to factor back into its components. An RSA keypair consists of a public key used to encrypt and a private key used to decrypt. The public key can be freely shared without compromising security, because deriving the private key would require factoring a product of two 1024-bit or 2048-bit primes, a task far beyond current computational capability. RSA is the foundational technology underlying HTTPS, digital signatures, and secure email. The core algorithm works as follows: choose two large distinct primes p and q, then compute n equals p times q and φ of n, or Euler's totient function, equals the quantity p minus one times the quantity q minus one. Choose an integer e coprime to φ of n, typically e equals 65537, and compute d such that e times d is congruent to one modulo φ of n, using the extended Euclidean algorithm. The public key is the pair n and e, and the private key is the pair n and d. Publish n and e freely and keep d secret. To encrypt, the ciphertext c is congruent to plaintext to the e power modulo n. To decrypt, the plaintext is congruent to c to the d power modulo n. This works because c to the d power is congruent to m to the e power all to the d power, which is congruent to m to the ed power, which is congruent to m modulo n, by Fermat's Little Theorem. The security of RSA rests entirely on the computational hardness of integer factorization. Deriving d from the public key would require factoring n into p and q, a task with no known subexponential algorithm for large n. With 2048-bit keys, the product n is roughly 2048 bits, more than 600 decimal digits, making it infeasible to factor with known algorithms. However, if a quantum computer running Shor's algorithm is ever realized, RSA would be broken, a recognized threat that is motivating post-quantum cryptography research. In practical deployment, plaintext is never encrypted directly. Instead, it is padded via OAEP, which stands for Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding, to prevent deterministic ciphertexts and chosen-plaintext attacks. Digital signatures work by using the private key to sign and allowing anyone with the public key to verify. A signature equals plaintext to the d power modulo n, and verification checks that the signature to the e power is congruent to the plaintext modulo n. Key generation requires selecting p and q by generating large random numbers and testing them for primality using probabilistic tests like Miller-Rabin. Modular exponentiation is computed via fast exponentiation, also called binary exponentiation, which takes O of log of the exponent multiplications. It is still slow compared to symmetric algorithms like AES. RSA relies on Fermat's Little Theorem: if n equals p times q and the greatest common divisor of m and n equals one, then m to the φ of n power is congruent to one modulo n, ensuring that e times d congruent to one modulo φ of n makes decryption work. The extended Euclidean algorithm efficiently computes the modular inverse d in O of log n time. RSA revolutionized cryptography when it was published in 1977 by enabling secure communication without a pre-shared secret, the hallmark of public-key cryptography. Before RSA, parties needed to exchange secret keys in person or via a secure channel. With RSA, Alice can broadcast her public key globally, and anyone can send her encrypted messages that only she can decrypt. This asymmetry is why RSA powers TLS and HTTPS: a web server publishes its public key in a certificate, allowing browsers to encrypt session keys that only the server can decrypt. RSA's security has held for decades despite intense cryptanalysis, making it one of the most studied and trusted algorithms in existence. However, RSA is slower than symmetric encryption by orders of magnitude. Modern practice uses RSA only to exchange symmetric keys, then uses those keys to encrypt bulk data. The rise of quantum computing threatens RSA's security, motivating NIST, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, to standardize post-quantum algorithms. Lattice-based and code-based systems are the leading candidates to replace RSA in the post-quantum era.
